claims: Latent EF and drift rate factors each independently predict the general ADHD factor in a bifactor model of ADHD.
When both EF and drift rate are entered into the model, slow drift rate (but not EF) continues to predict elevated ADHD symptomology.
Slow drift rate represents a discrete cognitive correlate of ADHD, providing a more mechanistically specific explanation of cognitive deficits than broad EF measures.
Using drift rate to index task performance improves upon conventional approaches to measuring cognitive dysfunction in ADHD.
summary: This paper investigates whether slow drift rate, an index of evidence accumulation speed derived from the diffusion model, better predicts parent and teacher ratings of ADHD than standard metrics of executive functioning (EF). Using structural equation modeling in a sample of 201 children, the study found that while poor EF and slow drift rate each independently predicted higher general ADHD symptomology, only drift rate continued to significantly predict symptoms when both were included in the model. The authors conclude that drift rate is a superior, mechanistically specific cognitive predictor of ADHD compared to traditional EF measures.
